event: Elsie wakes to the bread smell; the market flower in its cup has gone soft overnight.
prose: Elsie woke to the bread smell and the ovens knocking below. The first thing she looked at was the sill. The pink carnation stood in its chipped teacup among the plants where she had put it, and it had gone soft in the night. Its head hung a little to one side over the rim of the cup. Two of its frilled petals had dropped onto the wood. Elsie got up in her shift and went and touched it with one finger. It was still pink. She turned the cup so it faced the window and the light.

event: She waters the plants and tells Sunny the lemon that today she wants a quest with flowers in it.
prose: She filled the jug and watered the plants one at a time. She came to Sunny last, because she had saved her news for Sunny. The little lemon tree stood glossy and upright in her pot, with two hard green lemons the size of thimbles. Elsie tipped the water in carefully round the stem. "No cellars today. And no dungeons, if I can help it. I want a quest with flowers in it. Out in the air. Real flowers, growing, with sky over them." Sunny's leaves shone. Elsie took that for agreement and set down the jug.

event: She laces the halter, pins the clip, and packs salve, bandages and her notebook.
prose: She washed at the basin and dressed by the round window. She laced the cream halter up the front, snug, and tied it off. She stepped into the sage skirt and buckled the belt with its pouches over it. She pinned the pink-and-white clip above her ear by feel. On the bed she packed the little satchel: the pot of salve, scraped down now to half; two clean rolls of bandage; and the blue notebook, flat against the side. She looked round the attic once more, at the carnation and the plants, and went down.

event: At the guild hall Tamsin is already at the F-rank notices with a finger on the moonbells.
prose: She came into the guild hall at half past eight, into the morning roar, and saw Tamsin at once. It was easy to see Tamsin. She was standing square in front of the F-rank notices with Margery over her shoulder, her copper curls blazing in a slant of sun from the high windows. She had one finger pressed flat to a single notice, as if it might try to get away from her. When she heard Elsie's boots she looked round and grinned, and kept her finger exactly where it was. "This one. Moonbells."

event: Tamsin says the apothecary on Mortar Lane wants open moonbells by morning, and pays on delivery.
prose: Elsie came and stood at her elbow and read it. Tamsin read it out anyway, over her, tapping each word. "Apothecary on Mortar Lane wants moonbells. Two dozen, open ones, not shut, delivered by morning. Six lanterns." She tapped the last line twice. "And she pays on delivery. Straight into your hand on her own doorstep, not a week later through the hall. I've done her work before. She's a sour old thing in a nightcap but she counts honest." She took her finger off the notice at last and looked at Elsie sideways. "What do you think?"

memory.fact: An apothecary pays on delivery, and the guild pays out later.
An apothecary pays on delivery, and the guild pays out later.
The moonbell notice is from the apothecary on Mortar Lane: two dozen open moonbells, by morning.
The moonbell notice is from the apothecary on Mortar Lane: two dozen open moonbells, by morning.

event: Elsie says her mother taught her moonbells: blue, night-blooming, brewed for fever.
prose: Elsie had gone very still, looking at the word. Moonbells. "My mother taught me moonbells. On the road. When I was small." She could see it as she said it: the wagon, the lamp, her mother's brown hands. "They're blue. Little blue bells, about so big," and she made a cup of her finger and thumb, "and they only bloom at night. She used to brew them for fever. A moonbell draught, with honey, for the bad fevers that the willow-bark couldn't touch. I used to hold the cup." She smiled. "I've only ever seen them dried."

memory.fact: Elsie's mother taught her moonbells: blue night-blooming flowers she brewed into fever draughts.
Elsie's mother taught her moonbells: blue night-blooming flowers she brewed into fever draughts.

event: She says they open all together at dusk and shut again by midnight, so it must be night.
prose: "They open all together. That's what she always said. All at once, at dusk, a whole bed of them at the same moment, like someone saying a word. And they're shut again by midnight. And a shut one's no use. You can't force it, and it won't brew." She turned to Tamsin with her eyes shining. "So it has to be night. We'd have to go out at dusk and pick them while they're open, and bring them back before morning." She looked at the notice. "That's flowers. Growing, with sky over them. That's exactly what I wanted."

memory.fact: Moonbells open all together at dusk, and are shut again by midnight.
Moonbells open all together at dusk, and are shut again by midnight.
Moonbells open only between dusk and midnight, and a closed moonbell is worthless to an apothecary.
Moonbells open only between dusk and midnight, and a closed moonbell is worthless to an apothecary.

event: Tilly arrives with her apron on the right way round and asks where moonbells grow.
prose: There was a quick patter of boots. Tilly arrived beside them a little out of breath, with her braids swinging and her goggles up on her head where they belonged. Her apron was on the right way round. Elsie looked at it, and at Tilly's face, and smiled at her. Tilly smiled back, a little shy. "Good morning. What are we looking at? Moonbells? What are moonbells? No, I know what moonbells are, they're in Harrow's Herbal, page two hundred and something. I mean where. Where do they grow?"

event: Tamsin says at the Glasswood's edge, an hour east of the east gate, in hollows under glass trees.
prose: "The Glasswood," Tamsin said. "At the edge of it. You go out the east gate and walk an hour east along the cart track, through the meadows, and there it is." She sketched it in the air with her free hand: the track, the line of trees. "They grow in the hollows under the glass trees. Down in the shade, in among the roots, where the ground dips. A good hollow, you'll get a whole bed of them." She grinned. "I know a good hollow." Tilly's face had gone thoughtful, then wary, and her hand went to the goggles on her head.

memory.fact: The Glasswood's edge is an hour's walk east of the east gate, along a cart track through meadows.
The Glasswood's edge is an hour's walk east of the east gate, along a cart track through meadows.
Moonbells grow in shady hollows at the Glasswood's edge, among the roots of the glass trees.
Moonbells grow in shady hollows at the Glasswood's edge, among the roots of the glass trees.
Moonbells grow in shady hollows at the Glasswood's edge, among the roots of the glass trees.

event: Tilly asks if the Glasswood is underground; Tamsin says it's all sky, and Tilly lights up.
prose:
"Is it— The Glasswood. It's a dungeon, isn't it. Is it underground? Is it down? Like the Underbloom?"

Tamsin laughed out loud. "Underground? It's a wood. It's trees. It's all sky." She flung her arm up at the high rafters. "Sky the whole way up, and stars at night, and the wind in it. You couldn't get further from underground if you tried."

Tilly lit up. Her whole face did it, all at once, like a lamp turned up. "Oh. Oh, good. Oh, then I'll come."

memory.fact: The Glasswood is a dungeon wood of glass-barked trees out past the east gate.
The Glasswood is a dungeon wood of glass-barked trees out past the east gate.

event: Cora comes out of the charcoal door as the clerk enters the party for the moonbells.
prose: They took the notice to the long desk. The clerk entered the party in his book for the moonbells, Fairweather, three names, and the hour, with his pen scratching. Before he had finished the last name the charcoal-painted door off the main hall opened. Cora came out of it, ledger under her arm, and crossed the hall straight to them, as if she had heard the word through the door. She came to a stop a step behind Elsie, in her place. "Moonbells. The Glasswood." Elsie turned and smiled at her.

event: Cora says she walks the Glasswood edge on patrols, and will walk it with them tonight.
prose:
"I walk the Glasswood edge," Cora said. "On the Wardens' patrols. I know it well, from the east gate to the white posts." She looked down at the notice in Elsie's hand and back up. "If the party is out there after dark, the Accord puts me out there with it. I'll walk it with you tonight." She paused. "I'll be at the east gate at half past five."

Elsie beamed at her. "Oh, good. I'm so glad. You'll know all the best paths."

changes.note: Bond: Cora 8 → 9 (kindness: Elsie's praise, she'll know all the best paths)

memory.fact: Cora has walked the Glasswood on Wardens' patrols, and knows its edge well.
Cora has walked the Glasswood on Wardens' patrols, and knows its edge well.
Cora has walked the Glasswood on Wardens' patrols, and knows its edge well.
Cora has walked the Glasswood on Wardens' patrols, and knows its edge well.

event: Tamsin says on summer nights a pack of bramblewolves hunts the edge.
prose: Tamsin had been leaning on Margery with her chin on the haft, listening. Now she straightened up. Her grin went away, and she looked at the three of them in turn. "There's a thing you should know. About the edge, at night. In the summer." She lowered her voice a little, though the people nearby were busy at the board. "There's a pack of bramblewolves that hunts the edge on summer nights. Lean things. Fur like brambles, all thorns, and eyes that shine in the dark like lamps. I've seen them twice. Heard them more than that."

memory.fact: On summer nights a pack of bramblewolves hunts the Glasswood's edge: lean, thorn-furred, lamp-eyed.
On summer nights a pack of bramblewolves hunts the Glasswood's edge: lean, thorn-furred, lamp-eyed.
On summer nights a pack of bramblewolves hunts the Glasswood's edge: lean, thorn-furred, lamp-eyed.

event: She says they fear fire and loud noise, and go for whoever runs.
prose: "They're frightened of fire. Fire and loud noise. Wave a torch at them, or shout, or bang something, and they'll back off. They don't like it at all." She held up one finger, very serious. "But they go for whoever runs. That's the thing to remember. If they come, you don't run. You run, you're the one they pick, and they're faster than you, every time." She looked at Tilly, not unkindly, and then at Elsie. "So if you see eyes, you stand still. You stand still and you let me deal with it."

memory.fact: Bramblewolves fear fire and loud noise, and go for whoever runs.
Bramblewolves fear fire and loud noise, and go for whoever runs.
Bramblewolves fear fire and loud noise, and go for whoever runs.

event: Tilly goes pale, then says she can make fire and she can certainly make noise.
prose: Tilly had gone pale. The light had gone out of her face as fast as it had come. She stood with both hands at her belt, holding on to her vials, her lips pressed tight. Elsie watched her swallow. Tilly's chin came up, the way it had at the Tipsy Heron. "Fire. And noise." She looked down at her belt, then at Tamsin. Her voice went small and fierce. "I can make fire. You've seen me make fire. And I can certainly make noise. I've made more noise than anybody at the College. They had to replace the windows."

event: Elsie asks Tamsin to come and sit with her on the bench by the board.
prose: Tamsin laughed and clapped her on the shoulder. Tilly staggered and laughed too. Elsie laughed with them. She looked at Tamsin's face, at the grin, and at the way Tamsin's free hand had gone, while she talked about the wolves, to the knuckle wraps on the other. It was turning them round and round. Elsie touched her arm. "Tamsin. Come and sit with me a minute. On the bench." She nodded at the long bench by the quest board. Tamsin looked at her, then leaned Margery against the board and came.

event: She asks: if the red comes tonight, may she try her Tether on Tamsin?
prose: They sat side by side on the bench, close, with the hall roaring round them and Tilly and Cora a little way off at the board. Elsie turned to face her and drew one knee up onto the bench. She had thought about how to say it all the way from the notice. "If the red comes tonight. If something hurts you out there, and the red comes. May I try my Tether on you? To reach you. Only if you say yes."

event: Elsie says a Tether is a pact, and the one bound can break it whenever she likes.
prose: Before Tamsin could answer: "It's a pact. A Tether. That's what it is, when I make it, I know that much. It's not a leash, whatever the name sounds like. It's a pact. And the one who's bound can break it whenever she likes. Any time. She only has to want to, and it's gone." Elsie put her hand on Tamsin's knee to make her look. "So you'd be the one holding the end of it, not me. You could drop it the moment you didn't want it. I won't keep it on you." She looked into Tamsin's face. "I only want to reach you."

memory.fact: A Tether Elsie makes is a pact the bound one can break at will.
A Tether Elsie makes is a pact the bound one can break at will.

event: Tamsin looks at her hands a long while and says she has always been alone in the red.
prose: Tamsin looked down at her own hands. She looked at them for a long time, at the wraps Elsie had tied on the floor of the Leftovers, at the scarred knuckles under them, turning them over in her lap. The hall went on roaring round them. When she spoke her voice was low and rough and not like her. "When the red's got me, it's only me in there. Always has been. Me and the red. I can't hear anyone. I can't hear my own name. People shout it, I know they do, they've told me after." She stopped. "I just don't hear it."

event: Then she says yes, try, and her ears go red to the tips.
prose: She lifted her head and looked straight at Elsie, with her green eyes very bright. "Yes. Try." It came out of her rough and sudden. "Try it. If the red comes, you try." Her ears went red. They went red as Elsie watched, the colour climbing from the lobes up, slow and deep, until they were scarlet to the very tips against her copper curls. Her jaw set hard. Elsie squeezed her knee. Her eyes stung. "Thank you."

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 12 → 17 (turning point: leave to Tether her in the red)

event: Elsie turns to Cora and asks if that is enough, under the Accord.
prose: Elsie turned on the bench and looked for Cora. She found her already looking back, standing a little way off at the board with the ledger under her arm. Of course Cora had been watching. Elsie got up and went to her, and Tamsin came after. "Cora. Tamsin's said I can use my Tether on her. Tonight, if the red comes and I need to reach her. She's agreed." She held Cora's grey eyes. "Is that enough? Under the Accord? I want to do it properly. I don't want there to be any question."

event: Cora asks Tamsin to say it again in front of her; Tamsin says it again, louder.
prose: Cora looked at her a moment, then past her at Tamsin. "Say it again. In front of me. In your own words." Tamsin's ears were still red. She stuck out her chin and squared her shoulders. "I give Elsie Fairweather leave to put her Tether on me, if the red comes. Tonight or any night. That's my say-so, and I'll say it to the guildmaster's face." Her voice rang off the rafters. The clerk at the desk looked up, and half the people at the quest board turned their heads.

event: Cora writes it in the ledger, and reads it back: leave given, Tamsin Reyes, before the guild.
prose: Cora opened the black ledger on her palm, there by the board, and uncapped her pen. She wrote, small and quick and exact, while the hall slowly went back to its business. She turned the ledger a little toward them and read it back. "Leave given. Tamsin Reyes, before the guild, in the hearing of the Warden, to the Enthraller Elsie Fairweather, for the skill Tether." She looked up. "That is enough." She closed the ledger. Elsie let out a long breath.

memory.fact: Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.
Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.
Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.
Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.
Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.
Before the guild, Tamsin gave Elsie leave to put her Tether on her if the red comes.

event: Cora says the hall's business is done till the east gate, and goes to the charcoal door.
prose: "Then the hall's business with the party is done until the east gate." Cora inclined her head to the three of them, the small exact bow. "Half past five." She turned and walked back across the hall to the charcoal-painted door, straight-backed, the crowd giving her room. She went in, and the door shut behind her. Elsie watched it close. Beside her, Tamsin let out a breath too, a big one, and rubbed the back of her neck with her wrapped hand. "Wardens. Every time, I feel like I've been caught stealing apples."

event: Tilly asks Elsie to help her brew flame and noise for tonight, if she doesn't mind sulphur.
prose: Tilly had come up beside Elsie and was hovering, with her hands knotted in her apron. "Elsie. Would you— only if you want, only if you're free— would you help me brew? For tonight. Flame, a lot of flame, more than I've got, and something for noise. A real noise. I've got the makings at my room but it goes so much faster with two, and you've got such steady hands." She stopped. "If you don't mind sulphur. It smells of sulphur. Everything does. I'm sorry."

event: Tilly's room on Pickle Row smells of sulphur and is mostly a bench of glass.
prose: Tilly's room was on Pickle Row, a narrow crooked street off a back canal, at the top of a narrow crooked boarding house, up four flights of stairs that leaned. When she opened the door the smell came out to meet them: sulphur, strong and yellow, and under it vinegar, something burnt, something like pears. The room was small and low, full of light from one big window, and most of it was a bench. The bench ran the whole length of the wall under the window. Every inch of it was glass: flasks, retorts, tubes and jars, glittering.

memory.fact: Tilly lodges in a boarding house on Pickle Row, in a room that smells of sulphur.
Tilly lodges in a boarding house on Pickle Row, in a room that smells of sulphur.

pictured.coverAfter: Tilly's room was on Pickle Row, a narrow crooked street off a back canal,

event: The only seat is the bed, so Elsie sits on it with her knees drawn up and watches.
prose: There was a narrow bed against the other wall under a patched quilt, a shelf of books and a burner on a stand. That was all. There was no chair. There was nowhere to sit at all but the bed. So Elsie sat on it, at the end. She pulled off her boots, drew her knees up under her skirt and wrapped her arms round them. Leaning her back against the wall, she watched. The quilt was soft and smelled of Tilly, of soap and soot and pears. Tilly looked at her sitting on her bed and went pink. She turned to the bench very fast.

event: Tilly brews fast and talks faster, and Elsie hands her things before she asks for them.
prose: Tilly brewed fast. She lit the burner and set three flasks going at once, moving between them like someone dancing. She talked faster than she brewed. "Salts first, always salts first. The College says spirits first, and the College is wrong, the College is wrong about nearly everything, and then there were the windows—" Elsie watched her hands. After a while she saw how the work went. When Tilly's hand went out for the little brass tongs, Elsie leaned off the bed and put them into it. When it went for the stoppers, Elsie had the stoppers. When it went for the blue jar, the blue jar was there.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 13 → 14 (kindness: Elsie helps her brew)

event: Tilly stops with a vial in the air and stares at Elsie, then at her own open hand.
prose: Tilly stopped. She stood with a vial held up in the air in one hand, halfway to the burner, the blue jar in her other hand. Slowly she turned round and looked at Elsie on the bed. Her mouth was open. She stared at Elsie, then down at her own free hand, held open in the air where the tongs and the stoppers and the jar had arrived in it, as if she expected it to explain itself. "How do you do that?" Her voice came out odd and high. "You keep doing that."

event: Elsie says she watches what Tilly reaches for; Tilly goes pink and drops the stopper.
prose: "I watch what you reach for. You look at a thing first, just before your hand goes. So I look where you look." Elsie smiled up at Tilly from the bed with her chin on her knees. Tilly stared at her. All at once she went pink, from her collar to her hairline. Her fingers jumped on the vial. The glass stopper she was holding slipped out of them and fell. It bounced on the floorboards with a bright little chime and rolled away under the bed. Tilly made a small strangled noise and dived after it.

event: By noon there are flame vials stoppered in a row, and a fat bang-flask Tilly carries like an egg.
prose: By noon there was a row of flame vials along the windowsill, stoppered and sealed with wax, a dozen of them, each the length of Elsie's finger. In each was a clear liquid that shivered when the light moved. And there was the noise. It was a fat round flask the size of a grapefruit with a long neck, corked, wired and sealed. Tilly carried it across the room to its nest of rags in a box, very slowly, with both hands cupped under it and her tongue between her teeth, the way a person carries an egg they have been told not to drop.

changes.note: Tilly experience 80 → 90 (judged: Brew, flame vials and a bang-flask)

event: They eat bread and cheese on the bed, and Tilly gets crumbs in Elsie's lap and brushes them out.
prose: They ate on the bed, because there was nowhere else to eat. Tilly had bread and a wedge of hard yellow cheese. She sat down cross-legged on the quilt beside Elsie, broke the bread in her hands and talked with her mouth full. Crumbs went everywhere. They went down Tilly's apron, across the quilt and into Elsie's lap, on her bare thighs below the hem of the sage skirt. Tilly noticed. "Oh, sorry, sorry." Without thinking she reached over and brushed them off, quick little strokes of her fingers across Elsie's skin.

event: Tilly's hand stops on Elsie's knee, and she takes it back as if burnt.
prose: Her hand stopped. It stopped on Elsie's knee, mid-stroke, and stayed there, small and warm and a little rough at the fingertips from the burns, resting on the bare skin just above Elsie's knee. Tilly looked down at it as if it were someone else's hand. When she looked up her face was very close and very pink, and her blue eyes were wide. Elsie smiled at her. Tilly snatched her hand back into her own lap as if Elsie's knee had been a hot stove. She held it there with her other hand and stared at the window.

event: Tilly asks if Elsie is frightened about tonight; Elsie says a little, about the wolves.
prose:
After a moment, still looking at the window: "Are you frightened? About tonight. You don't look it at all." Tilly picked at the cheese.

Elsie thought about it honestly; she could not have answered any other way. "A little. About the wolves. Not the dark, and not the wood. I'd like to see the wood." She brushed the last crumbs off her skirt herself. "But I keep thinking about them going for whoever runs. And about Tamsin, if one bites her." She looked at Tilly. "A little."

memory.fact: Elsie cannot lie.

event: Elsie walks home along the canal at mid-afternoon to rest before the night.
prose: In the middle of the afternoon, with the sun hot on the canal, Elsie walked home from Pickle Row by the waterside, with her boots on again and the sulphur still in her hair. Tilly had walked her to the bottom of the leaning stairs and waved her off from the door, then gone back up to watch the flasks. The canal was green and slow and sleepy. Boatmen dozed under hats. Elsie walked along the warm stones with her satchel bumping. She meant to go home and lie down and rest before the night, the way Tamsin had told them all to.

event: She lies in the attic with the round window open, wide awake.
prose: She lay down on the narrow bed in the attic in her shift, on top of the blanket, with the round window pushed wide open for the air. She shut her eyes. She opened them again. The sloped ceiling was warm above her. The canal sounds came in, and the bakery below was quiet in the afternoon lull. She shut her eyes. They came open again by themselves. She lay on her back and looked at the ceiling with her hands folded on her stomach, wide awake, her heart going a little quick. She could not make herself sleep at all.

event: She opens her window by wishing and reads the word Tether a long time.
prose:
So she stopped trying. She lay there and wished her window open, the way she had on the lake wall. It opened in the warm air over her, plain and clear.

She looked at the word Tether for a long time. It was an ugly word for a pact, she thought, the word for a rope on a goat. "Tether." She tried it under her breath and could not make it sound kind. She read the three names under Bonds again instead, and that was better.

event: She packs salve, bandages, bread and apples, and laces her boots tight.
prose: At half past four she got up and packed. Salve, what was left of it, and both rolls of bandage. A heel of bread wrapped in a cloth, and four apples from the paper bag on her shelf, one each, red and hard. She put the satchel on. Sitting on the bed, she laced her boots tight, right up to the top, double-knotted, the way her mother laced hers before a long road.

event: The east gate stands at the east end of the south canal, with a clerk's booth beside it.
prose: The east gate stood at the east end of the south canal, where the water ran out under a low arch in the city wall and the road ran out beside it under a high one. The great gates stood open in the evening light. Beside them was a little wooden booth with a guild sign over the window and a lamp already lit inside. The others were there before her: Tamsin leaning on Margery, Tilly with her box held against her chest in both arms, and Cora a little apart, exactly at half past five, with her ledger and her coat buttoned to the throat.

event: The clerk writes the party into his book, and Elsie pays him for the Glasswood licence.
prose: The clerk in the booth was an old man with spectacles on the end of his nose. He had a big book open on the sill in front of him. He wrote the party into it slowly, one name at a time, asking each, then the hour and the business, moonbells. Beside Cora's name he wrote Warden in the margin with a little flourish. "Licence for the Glasswood is a lantern a party. Paid going out." Elsie opened her purse and took out a silver lantern. She laid it in his dry old palm, and he bit it and dropped it in his box.

changes.note: One silver lantern for the party's Glasswood licence: 100 → 90 pips

memory.fact: A guild clerk in a booth at the east gate sells Glasswood licences and logs every party in and out.

event: He says F-rank goes a mile into the wood, to the white posts, and no farther.
prose: "F-rank." He peered at the tag on Elsie's belt over his spectacles, and then at the others. "Then you know the rule. F-rank goes a mile into the wood and no farther. There's a line of white posts, a mile in, painted white, you can't miss them even at night. You get to the white posts, you turn round." He wagged a finger at them. "Not one step past." Elsie put her hand on her heart. "Not one step. I promise." He grunted and waved them through.

memory.fact: F-rank may go a mile into the Glasswood, to a line of white posts, and no farther.
F-rank may go a mile into the Glasswood, to a line of white posts, and no farther.

event: They walk the cart track east through meadows, with the sun going down behind them.
prose: They went out under the great arch of the east gate and onto the cart track, and the city fell away behind them. The track ran east, rutted and dusty, between low hedges and wide meadows gone gold with evening, full of tall grass, poppies and moon daisies. Crickets were singing. The sun was going down behind them, behind the city. Their four shadows ran out long and thin along the track ahead of them, reaching for the wood. Elsie turned once and walked a few steps backwards to look at the city, all its towers gold.

pictured.coverAfter: They went out under the great arch of the east gate and onto the cart
pictured.setting: the cart track through the meadows

event: Tamsin walks beside Elsie and swings Margery, and is quiet for a whole field.
prose: Tamsin walked beside her, close on her right, with Margery over her shoulder. Now and then she swung the axe idly at the heads of the tall grass along the verge, and the seed heads flew. She did not say anything. She was quiet for a whole field, from one hedge to the next, which Elsie had not known Tamsin could be. Elsie glanced at her. Tamsin was looking straight ahead at the dark line of trees on the horizon, her face thoughtful and set. Every so often her free hand went to the wraps on the other.

event: Tilly walks with Cora and asks her about the white posts until Cora answers her.
prose: Behind them Tilly walked with Cora, holding her box, and Elsie could hear her. "But what are they made of? The posts. Are they stone? Wood? Who paints them? How often? Why white? Is there a reason? Has anyone ever gone past them by accident in the dark? What happens if you're standing on the line exactly?" Cora walked on in silence. Tilly went on asking. At about the third hedge Elsie heard Cora sigh, very quietly. "Limewashed. By the Wardens." "Oh!" Tilly was delighted.

event: The Glasswood rises ahead: trees with clear glass bark, chiming in the evening wind.
prose: The Glasswood rose ahead of them as the track climbed the last long meadow, and Elsie saw it properly for the first time. The trees were glass. Their trunks and branches were clear as window glass, every one, tall and slender and branching, with leaves of a pale green glass so thin the low sun came through them. The whole wood caught the last of the light, broke it up into gold and green and rose, and threw it back. And it was chiming. The evening wind moved in the branches, and the glass touched glass. The whole wood rang softly, high and sweet, like a thousand small bells.

memory.fact: The Glasswood is a wood of trees with clear glass bark, which chime when the wind moves them.
The Glasswood is a wood of trees with clear glass bark, which chime when the wind moves them.

pictured.coverAfter: The Glasswood rose ahead of them as the track climbed the last long meadow,

event: Elsie stops on the track with her mouth open, and Tilly takes her hand to see what she sees.
prose: Elsie stopped on the track. She stood quite still in the ruts with her mouth open and her hands hanging at her sides. She looked, and could not move. Something behind her ribs hurt, sweetly. She did not know she had stopped until Tilly bumped into her from behind. Tilly came round beside her and looked at her face. She took her hand and turned to look where Elsie was looking, holding on, as if to see it with her. They stood side by side on the track with their fingers laced together. "Oh," Tilly said softly. "Oh, Elsie."

event: Tamsin leads them along the edge to a shady hollow among the glass roots.
prose: "This way," Tamsin said, and led them off the track along the edge of the wood, where the meadow grass ran up to the first glass trunks and stopped. They walked in the chiming, with the trees on their left, catching the sunset. The ground began to dip and rise. After a while Tamsin turned in among the first of the trees. The light went green and gold, and the chiming was all round them. She stopped at the lip of a hollow: a deep, round, shady dip in the ground, among the great glass roots, where the light did not reach.

event: The moonbells lie shut and blue among the roots, a whole hollow of them.
prose: Elsie came to the lip beside her and looked down, and caught her breath. The hollow was full of moonbells. They lay all over the floor of it and up its sides, among the glass roots, hundreds of them on their thin stems, and they were shut: small tight blue buds hanging their heads, closed like folded hands, a dusky blue in the shade, like the sky just after the sun goes. A whole hollow of them. They were exactly as her mother had drawn them for her once in the dirt with a stick by the wagon wheel. "Moonbells. Look. All of them."

pictured.coverAfter: Elsie came to the lip beside her and looked down, and caught her breath.

event: They sit on the hollow's lip and eat apples while the light goes.
prose: They sat down on the lip of the hollow in a row, with their boots dangling over. Elsie took the apples out of her satchel and gave one to each of them, keeping one herself. Cora looked at hers a moment before she took it. They ate them in the last of the light, crunching, while the sun went down behind the glass trees. The gold went out of the trunks, and they turned pale and grey, then clear as water. The chiming softened as the wind dropped. A first star came out over the meadow behind them, low and bright.

event: At dusk the moonbells open all together, and the hollow turns pale blue.
prose: The dusk came down, blue and soft, and the moonbells opened. They opened all together. Every bud in the hollow lifted its head at once and unfolded with a faint silky sound like a breath let out, hundreds of small blue bells turning their faces up at the same moment. As they opened they began to glow. A pale blue light came out of them, soft and cool, filling the hollow from side to side like water filling a bowl, until the whole hollow shone pale blue under the dark glass trees. Their four faces on the lip of it were blue with it.

event: Elsie says that is exactly how her mother described it, and her eyes fill.
prose: Elsie's voice came out strange. "That's it. That's exactly it. That's how she said. All at once, like someone saying a word." She was holding her apple core in both hands in her lap, and she did not know it. Her eyes filled, all at once, and spilled over. She let them. She was thinking of her mother's voice in the wagon in the dark, telling her, and of her mother's hands and the cup she used to hold. She was thinking that her mother was on a road somewhere south, a long way off, and did not know Elsie was sitting here seeing it.

event: Glass-winged moths drift up out of the trees; Cora says they are glimmer moths and harmless.
prose: Something drifted up out of the trees, pale and slow. Another, and another. They were moths, big soft moths with wings of clear glass, veined like leaves. The blue light of the moonbells shone through their wings as they rose, so that they glittered. They drifted over the hollow in slow wavering spirals, dozens of them, chiming very faintly when two of them touched. Tilly flinched and ducked. "Glimmer moths," Cora said, from the end of the row, quietly, without moving. "They're harmless." A moth settled on her knee, and she let it.

memory.fact: Glimmer moths with glass wings drift through the Glasswood by night, and are harmless.
Glimmer moths with glass wings drift through the Glasswood by night, and are harmless.
Glimmer moths with glass wings drift through the Glasswood by night, and are harmless.

event: Elsie picks with her fingers among the roots and slices a fingertip on fallen glass.
prose: Elsie slid down into the hollow first, carefully, among the roots, into the blue light, and knelt among the moonbells. They were cool to the touch and smelled faintly of honey and rain. She began to pick them with her fingers, the way her mother had shown her, pinching each stem low down so the bell came away whole. She reached in under a great glass root for a fine one. Something sliced across the tip of her finger, quick and clean. She gasped and snatched her hand back. A curl of fallen glass lay in the moss. Her fingertip welled red.

event: Tamsin says fallen glass cuts like a knife, and gatherers here wear full gloves.
prose: "Let me see," Tamsin said. In one jump she was down in the hollow beside her, kneeling, taking Elsie's hand and turning it to the blue light. The cut was small and deep, right across the pad of her finger, and bleeding steadily. Tamsin hissed through her teeth. "Fallen glass. It's all over the floor in here, under the moss. It cuts like a knife. Sharper than a knife." She shook her head. "The gatherers that come out here wear full gloves. Leather, right up to the wrist. Not ones with the fingers cut off."

memory.fact: Fallen glass from the trees cuts like a knife, so gatherers in the Glasswood wear gloves.
Fallen glass from the trees cuts like a knife, so gatherers in the Glasswood wear gloves.

event: She unwinds one of her own knuckle wraps and binds Elsie's fingers in it, slow.
prose: She did not let go of Elsie's hand. She tucked it under her arm, against her side, to hold it still. With her other hand and her teeth she began to unwind one of her own knuckle wraps, the left one, the one Elsie had tied on the floor of the Leftovers. She took Elsie's hand back and wrapped the strip round her cut fingertip and round the next two fingers with it, slowly, carefully, over and under, the way Elsie had wrapped her knuckles. She did it with her head bent close. Her breath was warm on Elsie's wrist.

event: Elsie thanks her and Tamsin keeps hold of her hand a moment longer than the binding needs.
prose: "Thank you," Elsie said. Tamsin tied off the end of the wrap and tucked it under. But she did not let go. She held Elsie's bound hand in both of hers, in the blue light, a moment longer than the binding needed, then another moment, with her thumb resting on the inside of Elsie's wrist where the pulse was. She was looking down at their hands. Her ears were red in the blue light. She let go, quite suddenly, and stood up. "Mind the glass, all of you." It was gruff, and for the moonbells.

event: They gather in the bells' own pale glow, Elsie choosing full-open bells and Tilly counting aloud.
prose: They gathered by the light of the bells themselves. There was no need for any other. Elsie went among them choosing, bound fingers and all, picking only the ones full open, wide-mouthed and bright, and leaving the half-open ones to the moths. She laid each one into her satchel on a bed of moss, carefully, so they would not bruise. Tilly knelt beside her holding the satchel open, counting aloud in a whisper as each went in, "seven, eight, nine," losing count and starting again. Tamsin picked a few too, with her big careful hands.

event: Cora stands at the hollow's edge facing the wood, ledger shut, watching the trees.
prose: Cora did not come down into the hollow. Elsie looked up once, and saw her standing at the lip of it, against the dark trees, with her back to the moonbells. She was facing the wood. She stood straight and still in her charcoal coat with the ledger shut under her arm. She was watching the trees: watching between the glass trunks, into the dark, her head turning slowly from one side to the other and back. The blue light lit the back of her neck and the edge of her jaw. Elsie looked at her a while, then went back to picking.

event: A thornhare bolts from the roots and Tilly yelps; Tamsin says it bites only if cornered.
prose: Something burst out of the roots right at Tilly's knee, small and quick and spiny. It shot across the hollow in three great bounds and away under the trees. Tilly yelped and fell over backwards into the moonbells with her legs in the air. Tamsin laughed out loud, the first time she had laughed since the guild hall. "Thornhare." She hauled Tilly up by one arm. "That's all. Spiny little things. Rabbit, with prickles on. They'll only bite if they're cornered, and you didn't corner it, it cornered you." Tilly sat up pink, picking moss out of her braids.

memory.fact: Thornhares live at the Glasswood's edge: rabbit-sized and spined, they bite if cornered.
Thornhares live at the Glasswood's edge: rabbit-sized and spined, they bite if cornered.
Thornhares live at the Glasswood's edge: rabbit-sized and spined, they bite if cornered.

event: By half past eight Tamsin, who read the notice, says they have all it asks for, and a few to spare.
prose: At half past eight by the stars, or by Tamsin's feeling, which she said was better than the stars, Tamsin stood up in the hollow with her hands on her hips and looked at the satchel. "I read the notice. I know what the old woman wants." She counted the bells under the moss with one finger, her lips moving. "That's two dozen. Open ones, all of them, and a few over, for any that get crushed on the way. That's all she asked for." She grinned at Elsie. "We're done. We can go home."

event: Lamp-eyed shapes stand up between the glass trunks, lean and thorn-furred.
prose: She stopped grinning. Elsie saw her face change and turned to see what she was looking at, out beyond the lip of the hollow, between the glass trunks. There were eyes. Pairs of eyes, low down in the dark between the trees, round and yellow and shining like lamps. As Elsie looked, the shapes under the eyes stood up. They were lean, long-legged, long-jawed, and their fur stood up all over them in spikes and hooks like a hedge of brambles, black against the faint blue glow. There were five. Six. More, further back.

event: Tamsin says, quiet, bramblewolves; stand still, all of you.
prose: "Bramblewolves." It was very quiet and very calm, in a voice Elsie had not heard Tamsin use. She was already moving, sliding Margery off her shoulder into both hands, stepping up to the lip of the hollow, putting herself between the eyes and the three of them. Without turning her head: "Stand still. All of you. Don't move. Don't run. Stand right where you are." Cora had not moved at all. She stood exactly where she had stood, and her eyes were on the wolves.

event: Tilly's feet start to turn; Elsie takes her hand hard and holds her where she stands.
prose: Tilly made a sound beside her, a thin high sound, and Elsie felt her move. Tilly's feet had started to turn. Her whole body was turning away from the eyes, toward the meadow, toward the open, the way a body turns before the mind has decided anything. In one more breath she would be running. Elsie caught her hand. She caught it hard and held it. She pulled Tilly in against her side and held her there where she stood. Into her ear, low and quick: "No. Stay. Stay with me. Stand still. I've got you. I've got you."

event: Tilly lights a flame vial and throws it, and fire runs along the leaf litter.
prose: Tilly stood. She was shaking all over against Elsie's side, but she stood. With her free hand, without letting go of Elsie, she reached to her belt and pulled a flame vial out of its loop. She bit the wax off the top and spat it. Something hissed inside the glass. She drew back her arm and threw it, hard, out over the lip of the hollow toward the eyes. It burst on a glass root in a splash of light. Fire ran out from it across the dry leaf litter under the trees, a low quick river of flame, crackling, bright gold.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 14 → 17 (danger shared: Elsie held her still before the wolves)

event: The pack circles wide of the fire, and one comes round at Tilly's open side.
prose: The wolves flinched back from the fire. They did not run. They split and went round it, wide, in a long loose circle through the trees, their thorny backs catching the firelight, their lamp eyes turned toward the hollow. Elsie turned with them, holding Tilly. They were coming round. The fire was on the hollow's near side, and Tamsin was on its far lip. One of the wolves had gone wide round the end of the fire. It was coming in low and fast out of the dark at the side where Tilly stood, where there was no fire and no axe.

event: Tamsin steps across it with Margery; the wolf's teeth catch her forearm.
prose: Tamsin saw it. She came along the lip of the hollow in three long strides and stepped across in front of Tilly with Margery up, between Tilly and the wolf, as it sprang. She swung the haft across her body to block it. The wolf twisted in the air and caught her instead. Its long jaws closed on her bare forearm above the wrap. Elsie heard the teeth go in. Tamsin shouted, a short ugly shout, and staggered with the weight of the beast hanging off her arm, its thorny body thrashing against her side.

event: Tamsin's eyes go flat, all at once, and the red has her.
prose: Tamsin's eyes went flat. Elsie saw it, in the firelight, close: it happened all at once this time, not slowly as it had in the cellar, the way a candle goes out. The green went out of them. What was left was blank and shining and looked through everything. Tamsin's lips pulled back from her teeth. Her whole body changed shape, somehow, swelled and set. A sound came out of her that was not a word, low and terrible, out of the bottom of her chest. The red had her. Elsie knew it the way she would know a fever.

event: She throws the wolf off and turns with the axe up, and Elsie is the nearest thing to her.
prose: Tamsin wrenched her arm up and flung the wolf off it, clean off, through the air. It hit a glass trunk with a ringing crack and fell. She turned. She turned with Margery up in both hands, high over her head. Her blank eyes went across the hollow looking for the next thing that moved, and the nearest thing that moved, the nearest thing to her in all the blue light and firelight, was Elsie. Elsie was standing a single step away with Tilly behind her. The axe blade hung in the air above her, catching the fire.

event: Elsie stands her ground; she reaches for Tamsin, and asks for her Tether.
prose: Elsie did not step back. She let go of Tilly's hand and pushed her gently behind her. She stood her ground in the moonbells and looked up at Tamsin under the axe. She was frightened. She was frightened all the way through, and she found that it did not matter at all. She held out both her hands to Tamsin, open, the bound one and the bare one, reaching for her. Inside herself she reached too. She reached for the word she had read so long in the attic, and asked for it. Please, she thought. Tether. Let me reach her.

event: A window opens in the dark above them: Tether.
prose:
A window opened in the dark over their heads, small and clear, its light falling across the two of them and the axe between. Elsie had asked, and here it was. It hung in the air above Tamsin's raised arms, steady as a lamp, white against the dark glass trees, while the fire crackled, the moonbells glowed and the wolves' eyes moved behind it in the dark.

:::skill
name: Tether
:::

event: A thread of light runs from Elsie's chest to Tamsin's, thin as a hair and warm.
prose: Something left her. Elsie felt it go out of the middle of her chest, just under her breastbone, warm, the way warmth goes out of a hand into another hand held in winter. A thread of light ran from her to Tamsin. It was thin as a hair, gold and warm. It ran straight and true through the air between them, from Elsie's chest to Tamsin's. It settled there, over Tamsin's heart, and held. Elsie could feel it, the whole length of it, like holding one end of a string in the dark and feeling someone at the other end.

event: Tamsin stops with the axe high; her flat eyes find Elsie through the red.
prose: Tamsin stopped. She stopped with the great axe high over her head, poised, every muscle in her arms standing out, and stayed there. Her chest heaved. Her blank eyes moved. They came down off the dark and wandered. They found the thread, followed it, and found Elsie at the end of it. They were still flat. The red was still in them. But they were looking at her, at Elsie, and Elsie saw that Tamsin knew her. Somewhere in there, inside the red, Tamsin knew exactly who she was. "Tamsin. It's me."

changes.note: Experience: 90 / 100 (judged: first Tether, reached Tamsin in the red)

event: She turns her back on her party, and sets herself between them and the wolves.
prose: Tamsin turned her back. She swung round, away from Elsie, with the axe still up, and planted her feet in the moonbells at the lip of the hollow facing out. Elsie, Tilly and Cora were behind her. In front of her was the dark wood, and the wolves in it. She set herself there like a wall, between them and the wolves. The thread ran out from Elsie's chest to her back, gold and steady. The red was still on her. Elsie could see it in every line of her body. But she had chosen which way to face.

event: Inside the red she fights only wolves, and keeps the axe clear of her own.
prose: The wolves came. Two of them came at her out of the dark at once, and Tamsin met them, roaring. Margery went round in a great flashing arc, and the first wolf went tumbling back into the trees. Tamsin fought in a fury, blind and huge and terrible. But she fought only wolves. When she swung, she swung out, at the dark, at thorn and lamp-eye, and the axe did not come back toward the hollow. She kept the blade clear of her own, every stroke, as if she could see the thread too.

memory.fact: Held by a Tether from Elsie, Tamsin in her Frenzy knows her own party from foes.
Held by a Tether from Elsie, Tamsin in her Frenzy knows her own party from foes.

event: Tilly throws the bang-flask; the noise cracks the glass trees and they ring like bells.
prose: "Cover your ears!" Tilly screamed behind her. Elsie turned and saw her standing up in the moonbells with the fat round flask raised in both hands, her face white and fierce in the firelight. She threw it. It went over Tamsin's head in a high arc, out into the dark between the trees, and burst. The noise was enormous. It hit Elsie in the chest like a door slammed on her, a great flat crack that shook the ground. Every glass tree in the wood rang with it, all together, trunk and branch and leaf, a huge wild clamour like every bell in a city struck at once.

event: The pack breaks at the fire and the noise and runs into the wood.
prose: The pack broke. Elsie saw them go, the lamp eyes all turning at once, the thorny bodies wheeling, between the fire on one side, the ringing glass on every side and the roaring thing with the axe in front of them. They ran. They fled back into the wood, yelping, a long scatter of shapes and eyes going away between the trunks, smaller and smaller, until the eyes were gone. The glass trees went on ringing after them, slowly quieter, like the ringing in an ear. The fire crackled low along the leaf litter.

changes.note: Tamsin experience 70 → 80 (judged: fought the bramblewolves off)
Bond: Tamsin 17 → 20 (danger shared: the bramblewolves)
Bond: Cora 9 → 12 (danger shared: the bramblewolves)

event: Tamsin stands swinging at nothing until the red burns out, and then she drops to her knees.
prose: Tamsin did not stop. She stood at the lip of the hollow with her back to them. She went on swinging Margery at the empty dark, great sweeping strokes at the trees where the wolves had been, roaring at them, while the thread hung gold between her back and Elsie's chest. Elsie stood and held her end of it. It went on for what felt like a long time. Then the strokes got slower, and the roaring stopped. Tamsin's arms came down. The axe head dropped to the ground, and Tamsin dropped too, onto her knees in the moonbells, and bent over.

event: Elsie feels an ache in her own forearm that is not hers, and knows where Tamsin is hurt.
prose: Elsie's own forearm hurt. She looked down at it in surprise. There was nothing on it: the skin was pale and whole in the blue light, and yet it ached, a deep hot throbbing ache just below the elbow on the inside of the arm, as if something had bitten it. But it was not hers. She was sure of it. It was coming to her along the thread, from the other end. It was Tamsin's. She knew, all at once and quite certainly, exactly where Tamsin was hurt, as if she had been told.

memory.fact: Elsie can feel when someone bound to her is hurting.
Elsie can feel when someone bound to her is hurting.

event: She kneels and finds the wolf bite on Tamsin's forearm, exactly where the ache is.
prose: She ran to her and knelt in the moonbells in front of her. She took her arm in both hands and turned it to the light. The wolf bite was there, on the inside of the forearm just below the elbow, in exactly the place where the ache sat in Elsie's own arm: a ragged double row of punctures, deep, bleeding freely down Tamsin's wrist and into the wrap. Elsie pressed her palm flat over it to slow the blood. Tamsin was shaking. She lifted her head, slowly. Her eyes were green again, and wet, and looking straight at Elsie.

changes.note: Bond: Tamsin 20 → 22 (Tether: back from the Frenzy along it)

event: Tamsin says she heard Elsie in there, in the red, the whole time.
prose: "I heard you." Tamsin's voice was hoarse and broken from the roaring, hardly a voice at all. "In there. In the red." She stared at Elsie as if she were something impossible. "I heard you. The whole time. You were there, the whole time, like— like someone saying my name in the next room. I couldn't stop. I couldn't come out. But I could hear you, and I knew which ones were mine." Her breath shook. "I knew which ones were mine, Elsie. I knew it was you behind me."

memory.fact: Held by a Tether from Elsie, Tamsin in her Frenzy knows her own party from foes.

event: Elsie says she can break the Tether whenever she likes; Tamsin says, leave it.
prose:
Elsie kept her palm pressed over the bite. "You can break it. The Tether. Now, whenever you like. You only have to want to, and it's gone, I promise you it is. I don't need to keep it now the wolves are gone." She could feel the thread still, warm under her breastbone, running to Tamsin's chest.

Tamsin looked down at it, as if she could see it, then up at Elsie, and her jaw worked. "Leave it. Leave it on. Don't you dare take it off." Her hand closed over Elsie's on her arm and held it there.

memory.fact: Elsie's Tether binds Tamsin, and Tamsin asked her to leave it on.
Elsie's Tether binds Tamsin, and Tamsin asked her to leave it on.
Elsie's Tether binds Tamsin, and Tamsin asked her to leave it on.
Elsie's Tether binds Tamsin, and Tamsin asked her to leave it on.

event: Cora opens her ledger by Tilly's flame and writes, and reads it aloud to Elsie.
prose: Cora came down into the hollow. She came and crouched by Tilly, who had sat down hard in the moonbells. She lit Tilly's little blue flame from her belt to see by, holding it out in her gloved hand. In its light she opened the black ledger on her knee and wrote. Elsie watched her across the hollow. Her pen moved small and quick and steady. Cora turned the ledger toward the flame and, without being asked, read it aloud, to Elsie, across the moonbells, in a voice that rang a little in the hush after the glass.

event: Skills used: Tether, on Tamsin Reyes, by her leave, given before the guild.
prose: "Fourth of the month. The Glasswood edge, by night. Skills used: Tether. On Tamsin Reyes. By her leave, given before the guild this morning in the Warden's hearing." She paused. "Duration, from the bite to now. Effect observed: the subject in Frenzy fought the attacking animals and turned from her party." She lifted her grey eyes from the page and looked at Elsie, kneeling in the moonbells with her hand on Tamsin's arm. "That's what I've written." She looked down again.

memory.fact: Held by a Tether from Elsie, Tamsin in her Frenzy knows her own party from foes.

event: Then Cora writes another line, and turns the page before Elsie can see it.
prose: Then she wrote another line. Elsie saw the pen go back to the page and move again, under what she had read, a single line, slower than the others, as if she were choosing every word. Cora did not read that one out. When she had finished it she lifted the pen and looked at it a moment. Before Elsie could see it or ask, she turned the page over, flat, so that the line was hidden underneath. She smoothed the clean page with her gloved hand, closed the ledger on it, and stood up.

memory.fact: At the Glasswood Cora wrote one more ledger line and hid it from Elsie.

event: In the empty ranger's hut at the edge, Elsie cleans and bandages Tamsin's arm.
prose: "There's a ranger's hut a few hundred yards along the edge. Empty. It's kept open for licensed parties." Cora led them to it through the trees with Tilly's flame held up: a little stone hut with a turf roof and a door on a latch. Inside were a bench, a table and a cold hearth, smelling of old smoke. Elsie sat Tamsin on the bench and lit the stub of candle on the table from Tilly's flame. She cleaned the bite with water from her flask and the last of the salve, and bandaged it, neat and firm.

memory.fact: An empty ranger's hut sits at the Glasswood's edge, open to any licensed party for shelter.

event: Tilly sits pressed against Elsie's other side and keeps hold of her sleeve.
prose: Tilly sat down on the bench on Elsie's other side, pressed right up against her, hip to hip, so close that Elsie could feel her trembling still through both their clothes. She did not say anything. She had a fistful of Elsie's skirt at the hip, the way a person keeps hold of a sleeve in a crowd. She did not let go of it while Elsie worked, not even when Elsie had to reach across for the bandage and Tilly's arm went with her. Elsie leaned into her a little, to tell her it was all right. Tilly leaned back, hard.

event: Elsie opens her own window, and under Tether it reads a name now: Tamsin.
prose:
When the bandage was tied, Elsie sat back between them on the bench and wished her window open, there in the candlelight, to see.

Under Tether there was a name now. Tamsin. Elsie looked at it a long time, the two words side by side, the ugly one and the dear one. She found that the ugly word did not look so ugly with Tamsin's name beside it. She read the name again.

event: They walk the cart track back under the stars, the moonbells glowing in the satchel.
prose: They walked back along the cart track under the stars, the four of them, with the meadows silver and breathing on either side and the crickets loud. The city was a low line of lights far ahead. Behind them the Glasswood chimed faintly, settling. Elsie carried the satchel against her hip with one hand over the flap. Through the canvas the moonbells glowed, a soft blue light leaking out at the seams, so that she walked in a little pool of it along the dark track. The moths came after her for a while, then gave up.

event: Tamsin walks so close to Elsie that their arms touch the whole way, and both let them.
prose: Tamsin walked beside her, close on her right as she had coming out. But closer now. So close that their arms touched, Tamsin's bandaged forearm against Elsie's bare one, skin to skin, all the way down the track, field after field, with every step. Neither of them moved away. Elsie did not want to, and Tamsin did not seem to want to either. Tamsin's arm was warm. Once, in the dark between two hedges, Elsie felt her shiver, all through, though the night was warm. The thread ran between them, gold and quiet. Elsie kept her arm where it was.

event: At the east gate the clerk writes the party out of his book.
prose: The east gate stood open still, with the lamp lit in the clerk's booth. The old man was there, spectacles on his nose, nodding over his book. He jerked awake as they came under the arch. He looked at them over his spectacles, all four, counting, then at Tamsin's bandaged arm and the satchel glowing at Elsie's hip, and grunted. "All back." He sounded faintly surprised. He found their names in the big book and wrote them out, one by one, with the hour beside each. "Good. Go home." "Thank you," Elsie said.

event: The apothecary on Mortar Lane opens in her nightcap and counts the open bells.
prose: The apothecary's shop on Mortar Lane was dark, with its shutters up and a brass mortar hanging over the door. Tamsin hammered on the door with her good fist until a window opened upstairs. A sour old face in a nightcap looked out and said several things. Then the door opened. The apothecary stood on the step in her nightgown and cap with a candle. Without a word she held out her hand for the satchel, and counted the moonbells into a basket one by one, holding each up to the candle to see it was open. Every one was.

event: She pays on the step, and Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly each pocket a third.
prose: At last: "Two dozen, and a few over." She sniffed, and looked at them all as if they had done it mainly to get her out of bed. She went in, came back and counted six silver lanterns out of a leather bag into Elsie's palm, there on the step, by candlelight. "Pays on delivery," Tamsin murmured. Elsie divided them on the doorstep: two to Tamsin, who pocketed them with a grin, two to Tilly, who tucked them into her apron, and two for herself, cool and heavy in her hand, into her purse.

event: Cora says she is off duty, and stands a moment, and goes up the lane alone.
prose: Cora had been standing a little apart, at the edge of the candlelight. Now, to Elsie: "I'm off duty." For a moment it seemed that was all. But she did not go. She stood there a moment longer, in the dark lane, with her ledger under her arm, looking at Elsie on the step. Her face in the candlelight was quite still and unreadable. Then she turned and went away up Mortar Lane alone, straight-backed, her boots quiet on the cobbles, until the dark took her.

event: Tilly hugs Elsie, then Tamsin, then runs for Pickle Row with her braids flying.
prose: Tilly hugged Elsie. She threw both arms round her neck, hard, box and all, so that the empty box dug into Elsie's back, and held on. When she let go she was pink to the ears. She turned and hugged Tamsin too, more carefully, round the waist, mindful of her arm. Tamsin patted her head. Tilly turned and ran for Pickle Row, light and quick down the dark lane, her braids flying out behind her and her empty box under her arm. She turned once at the corner to wave, and was gone.

event: Tamsin walks Elsie to the Honeycomb door and says goodnight twice.
prose: Tamsin walked Elsie home. She did not ask. She simply turned along Thimble Canal when Elsie did and walked beside her under the lanterns, close, with their arms touching, all the way to the Honeycomb's dark door. Elsie stopped on the step and turned round. Tamsin stood on the cobbles below her, which made their faces level. "Goodnight." Then she did not go. She stood there with her bandaged arm held against her chest and her curls wild. "Goodnight." Quieter. She still did not go.

event: Elsie says she loves her, and Tamsin stands very still on the step.
prose: "I love you." Elsie had felt it all the way home along the thread, and it was too big to keep in. "I love you, Tamsin. You came back for us. You turned round." Tamsin stood very still on the cobbles. She stood absolutely still, the way she had on the floor of the Leftovers, the way she had in the cellar, with her lips parted and her green eyes on Elsie's face in the lantern light. Her ears were going red. She did not say anything at all. Then she turned and walked away fast along the canal.

event: In the attic Elsie unwinds Tamsin's knuckle wrap from her finger and lays it on the sill.
prose: The attic was dark and warm and smelled of the carnation. Elsie lit the candle and sat on the edge of the bed with her boots still on. Her bound fingers had stiffened on the walk home. She began to unwind the strip of cloth from them, slowly, round and round, the way Tamsin had wound it on in the hollow with her head bent close. The cut under it had closed. The wrap was warm from her hand and a little stained with blue from the moonbells. She smoothed it out flat across her knee. She got up and laid it on the sill by the round window, beside the carnation in its cup, straight and careful, where the canal lanterns shone on it.
